title: Where do I start reading the Bible?
seoTitle: Where to Start Reading the Bible, and How to Keep Going
description: Start with the Gospel of Mark, a chapter a day. A pastor's plain guide to where to begin, which translation to choose, and what to do with the hard parts.
summary: Start with Mark, a chapter a day. Where to begin, which Bible to choose, and what to do when it's confusing.
askedAs: where to start reading the Bible
which Bible translation should I read
what book of the Bible should I read first
read the Bible in a year
the Bible is hard to read
answer: You want to read the Bible, maybe for the first time, maybe for the first time in years, and you don't know where to begin. Or you tried once, started on page one, and quietly gave up somewhere in the laws of Leviticus. That isn't a failure of faith or intelligence. The Bible is a library, sixty-six books in a Protestant Bible, and you don't have to start a library at the first shelf. Start with the Gospel of Mark, the shortest account of Jesus' life. Read one chapter a day at the same time and place, and write down one question each day. Then read Genesis, with a psalm alongside. Any major modern translation you understand will do, and [the Study Bible](/study/bible) here is free. If you can, read with one other person.
happening:
Most people begin the Bible the way they'd begin any book, at the first page. Genesis holds you for a while, with its good world and its garden, its flood, and a family that lies and schemes and is chosen anyway, and Exodus carries you out of Egypt. Then the book changes under you. The last chapters of Exodus measure out a tent for worship in close detail, Leviticus spends whole chapters on sacrifices, skin diseases, and mildew, and Numbers opens with a census. You read a few more days out of duty, miss one, miss three, and the bookmark stays where it is. What lingers is a quiet verdict about yourself: other people seem able to do this, and you can't.

Other people come in by other doors. One opens to a random page and lands in a genealogy or a battle. Another grew up with verses on the refrigerator and has never read a single book of the Bible from beginning to end. A skeptic wants to know what is actually in the book everyone argues about. And someone else is coming back to a Bible that was once used against them, not sure they can open it without flinching.

The usual explanations each hold something true. One says you need discipline: pick a plan, set a reminder, keep the streak. Habits matter, but a streak can't tell you why you got lost in Leviticus. Another says the Bible is too hard without training. It is ancient, and good notes help, yet much of it was first read aloud to ordinary people, and anyone can follow Mark. A third says that if you really loved God you'd love this book, so your trouble reveals a cold heart. Christians do believe God speaks through Scripture and helps us understand it by his Spirit, but the Bible also shows people who loved God and still didn't understand what they were reading until someone opened it to them.

The skeptic says the Bible is an anthology of old texts by many hands, and that much is true: it was gathered over centuries, and its writers don't all sound alike. What that misses is the shape. Read whole, the collection tells one story, from a good world made by God, through its breaking, through God's long work with one family and one nation, to Jesus, and on to a world made new. Read in pieces, it looks like a heap, and only when you follow the story do the pieces begin to find their places.

What every explanation leaves out is simpler. Most of us were never shown the door. Nobody told us we could begin in the middle of the library, that the story has a center, or that for most of its history this book has been read aloud, in company. The trouble usually isn't you. It's the way the book was handed to you.

scripture.intro: The Bible has a surprising amount to say about reading the Bible. It shows people with the Scriptures in hand who still can't make sense of them: two grieving disciples whom Jesus calls slow to believe and then teaches for the rest of the road, and an official who asks for a guide and is given one. Neither is sent away for needing help. The Bible is just as plain about what the reading is for.

passages.text: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. ... I am severely afflicted, O LORD; revive me through Your word.
passages.reading: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, twenty-two stanzas of eight verses, one stanza for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Its writer loved God's word enough to spend 176 verses on it, and the famous line about the lamp comes two verses before a cry of severe affliction. The lamp isn't decoration for a good day. It's what you hold up in the dark, and in that world it was a small clay dish of oil that lit a few steps at a time. You won't understand the whole Bible before you begin, and you don't need to. A lamp only has to light the next step.

passages.text: And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself. ... They asked each other, “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?”
passages.reading: On the first Easter, two followers of Jesus are walking about seven miles to a village called Emmaus, sad and confused. They had hoped he would redeem Israel, he has been crucified, and the report of an empty tomb makes no sense to them. A stranger falls into step beside them. It's Jesus, though they don't recognize him, and he begins with their Bible, the Scriptures Christians now call the Old Testament, showing them what it had said about him all along. That's the best reason to begin with a Gospel: you meet the center of the story first, and the rest of the library arranges itself around him. Their eyes are opened only when he breaks bread at their table, and then they realize their hearts had been burning all along the road while he opened the Scriptures to them.

passages.text: So Philip ran up and heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet. “Do you understand what you are reading?” Philip asked. “How can I,” he said, “unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. ... Then Philip began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.
passages.reading: The man in the chariot was a senior official in charge of the treasury of the queen of the Ethiopians. He had traveled a long way to worship in Jerusalem, and on the road home he was reading Isaiah aloud, which is how Philip heard him. He was educated, powerful, and devout, and he still couldn't make sense of a poem about someone led like a sheep to the slaughter. His answer to Philip is one of the most honest sentences in the Bible, and nothing in the story suggests he was ashamed to say it; he simply made room beside him for a guide. Philip began with the very passage the man was stuck on and led from there to Jesus. Farther down the road, the man asked to be baptized (Acts 8:36).

passages.text: But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed, since you know from whom you have learned them. From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work.
passages.reading: These verses are usually quoted in arguments about the Bible, but their setting is personal. The letter presents itself as Paul's farewell, written from prison as he expected to die (2 Timothy 4:6), to a younger man he calls his beloved child. Paul reminds Timothy that he knows whom he learned from, and the letter has already said where his faith began: it lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5). Timothy's father was a Greek (Acts 16:1), and the letter never mentions him. Then Paul says what Scripture is for: to make a person wise for salvation through faith in Christ, and ready for every good work. If no one read the Bible to you as a child, you can begin now. In every family, someone has to be the first.

whyHard:
Some of the difficulty is real, and the skeptic is right to name it. The Bible is a library written across many centuries, in three languages, in the forms of the ancient world: law codes, genealogies, war stories, love poems, prophetic visions, and letters to churches long gone. Some of it is hard to follow, and some of it is hard to bear. Scripture even says so about itself: “Some parts of his letters are hard to understand,” Second Peter says of Paul (2 Peter 3:16). A page that pretended otherwise wouldn't deserve your trust.

Still, the ancient world isn't the only thing that stops people. Part of it is the shape the book often arrives in: two columns of small type with a number in front of nearly every sentence, a page that looks more like a legal code than a story. Those numbers weren't there when it was written. The chapters are medieval, traditionally credited to Stephen Langton, a teacher in Paris who became Archbishop of Canterbury early in the thirteenth century. The New Testament's verse numbers came later still, from the printer Robert Estienne, whose Greek New Testament of 1551 was the first to number its verses the way ours are numbered. They're useful the way street addresses are useful. But once every sentence had its own number, it became easy to treat each one as a freestanding saying, something you could lift out and carry away without the paragraph it lived in.

And we carried them away, onto mugs and calendars and graduation cards, into sympathy texts and political arguments. One of the best-loved promises in Scripture, “I know the plans I have for you” (Jeremiah 29:11), sits in a letter telling exiles in Babylon to build houses, plant gardens, and pray for the city that held them, because Babylon's seventy years had to run their course, and many who first heard it would die before it was kept. In its setting the promise is harder and deeper, and a coffee mug can show you neither. Every tribe handles the Bible this way, left and right, and preachers do too. I'm a preacher, and it's easier than it should be to build a sermon on one sentence without asking what that sentence was doing where it lives.

Then there's the way we now read everything: in scraps, a few seconds at a time, on screens built to move us along. A verse over a photograph of a sunset fits that world perfectly. Leviticus doesn't, and neither does a letter like Colossians, written to be read aloud to a gathered church and then passed on to the next one (Colossians 4:16). We didn't exactly choose these habits, but we absorbed them, and they shape what feels readable.

Last comes fear: of reading it wrong, of landing on a terrible passage alone, of asking a question that shows how little you know. The church hasn't always helped. Sometimes we've made the Bible feel like an exam that insiders pass, and sometimes we've told people to ask only what a verse means to them, as if it had no author and no setting. Both leave the reader alone. For most of Christian history, believers knew Scripture mainly by hearing it read aloud when the church gathered, not by reading it alone. Reading it for yourself is a hard-won gift: copies of William Tyndale's English New Testament were burned in London in 1526, the year they arrived, and Tyndale himself was executed for heresy in 1536. Somewhere between that gift and the phone in your pocket, a lot of us ended up reading alone, if we read at all.

The fault lies less with the reader than with what we handed over. We gave people a library cut into numbered sayings, in a culture that reads in scraps, and left them to read it by themselves. Then we wondered why they quit.

thisWeek.intro: You don't need a system to begin, or to feel ready. You need a small practice you can repeat, about fifteen minutes a day. If you miss a day, pick up where you left off. The point is to keep company with the book, not to keep a streak.

steps.title: Pick a time and a place
steps.body: Choose the same time each day and tie it to something you already do: the first cup of coffee, a lunch break, the quiet after the kids are asleep. Sit where you won't be interrupted, and if you read on your phone, silence the notifications first, because the feed will always be louder than the book.

steps.title: Choose a Bible you can read
steps.body: Any major modern translation you understand is a good place to start. The [Study Bible](/study/bible) here uses the Berean Standard Bible, which is free, and the ESV, NIV, and NLT are common choices; the questions at the end of this page explain how they differ. Don't let the choice become a reason to wait.

steps.title: Read Mark, one chapter a day
steps.body: Open to [Mark 1](/study/bible/mark/1) and read the whole chapter. Mark is the shortest of the four accounts of Jesus' life, sixteen chapters, and it moves quickly. Read it aloud if you can, since much of the Bible was first heard that way. Don't stop to solve every puzzle. Watch what Jesus does, what he says, and how people respond to him.

steps.title: Write down one question
steps.body: Keep a notebook, or a note on your phone, just for this. Each day, write one question the chapter raises and one line that stopped you. The question can be simple (*who were the Pharisees?*) or hard (*why did Jesus answer her like that?*). You don't need to answer it yet. Writing it down turns a vague confusion into something you can carry to someone else.

steps.title: When a passage troubles you, ask four questions
steps.body: Sooner or later you'll hit something confusing or disturbing. Before you decide what it means, ask who wrote it, to whom, what kind of writing it is (a story, a law, a poem, a letter, a vision), and where it sits in the Bible's one story. That won't make every hard text easy, but it will keep you from reading a poem as a legal code or an ancient war story as orders for today. The Study Bible's book introductions and chapter notes help with all four.

steps.title: Find one person to read with
steps.body: Ask a friend, a spouse, or someone from church to read Mark with you, the same chapter each day, and text each other your question or your line. If you belong to a church, ask your pastor whether a group is reading together or whether someone would read with you; a good pastor will be glad you asked. If you don't have a church, one friend is enough to begin.

moreHelp.body:
For most people, trouble reading the Bible calls for a friend, a group, or a pastor. But for some the Bible is tangled up with harm. Some were shamed, threatened, or controlled with verses as children, in a church, or in a marriage, and opening the book brings back fear or memories that don't settle. Some find that reading about judgment sets off a dread they can't switch off, with hours spent checking, rereading, and confessing. Some are in a group or a home where Scripture is used to cut them off from family, demand total obedience, or excuse someone hurting them. None of that means your faith is weak. It means something heavier is going on, and it deserves real help alongside pastoral care.

A licensed counselor can help, and many are glad to work with a person's faith rather than against it. Ask your doctor for a referral, look in your insurer's directory, or ask a pastor you trust which counselors they know locally. If you want a Christian counselor, ask how their faith shapes their practice; with any counselor, check that they're licensed in your state. When Scripture is used to control or hurt you, that is spiritual abuse, and your safety comes first. The National Domestic Violence Hotline is there for anyone afraid of someone at home, and its number is on [Find Help](/help#help-now). If you're in danger, call 911. If you're thinking about ending your life, call or text 988 now.
signs: Reading Scripture brings back memories of abuse, or panic, nightmares, or dread that doesn't ease after a few days.
Fear that God can't forgive you fills hours of your day with checking, rereading, or confessing, and no reassurance lasts.
You can't sleep, eat, or work because of what reading stirs up. Start with your doctor.
Someone uses the Bible to control you, frighten you, or excuse hurting you. If you're in danger, call 911.
You've had thoughts of ending your life, or that others would be better off without you. Call or text 988.
A child tells you an adult used the Bible or the church to hurt them or keep them quiet. Call the police or child protective services.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't need the right words. You can say, *I've been trying to read the Bible, and it keeps bringing up things I can't carry alone. My faith matters to me, and I'd like help with this.* Then ask whether they're licensed in your state, whether they've worked with people whose faith is part of the picture, and how they'd handle it if your beliefs differ from theirs. A good counselor will answer plainly and won't push their faith, or their lack of one, on you.
moreHelp.cost: Counseling costs vary with where you live and the counselor's license, and insurance may cover part of it. If cost is a barrier, ask about sliding-scale fees, look for a community mental health center or a university training clinic, or see whether your employer's assistance program offers free sessions. Many churches have benevolence funds that can help. And the Bible itself shouldn't cost you anything: [the Study Bible](/study/bible) here is free, and many churches will give you a Bible if you ask.

helping.body:
If someone asks you where to start, the best thing you can offer is company. Most people need someone to read with, and permission to ask anything, far more than a lecture on method. Offer to read Mark together, a chapter a day, trading one question each day, and read aloud when you meet. When they ask something you can't answer, say so and look it up together; that honesty will teach them more than a quick answer would. Don't assume they know the story, the names, or the vocabulary, and never make them feel the gap.

Be careful with the hard parts. If they hit a violent story or a harsh law, don't hurry them past it or explain it away; say it's hard, read what's around it, and keep going together. If the Bible was once used against them, let them set the pace. Parents, read with your children, and let them see you read on your own. And if you lead a group or pastor a church, remember that some people in the room can't find Habakkuk and are ashamed of it, and some were hurt by people who could. Make the room safe for both.
say: Want to read Mark with me? A chapter a day, and we'll text each other one question.
I don't know. Let's find out together.
That passage bothers me too. Let's read what's around it.
Missed a few days? Just pick up where you left off.
dontSay: Just start at Genesis and read straight through.
That's not a real Bible translation.
If you really loved God, you'd want to read it.
helping.next: Get them a Bible they can read, or open [the Study Bible](/study/bible) with them on their phone and find Mark 1 together. Set a time to talk after the first week. If they want more, bring them into a group or a study like [The Story of the Bible](/studyguides/the-story-of-the-bible), which a volunteer can lead with no preparation. If reading stirs up old harm, don't try to be their counselor. Help them find one, and stay their friend.

prayer:
God, I don't know where to start. I've opened this book before and closed it, sometimes bored, sometimes lost, sometimes afraid of what I'd find. Some days I'm not sure I believe it. I'm asking anyway.

You walked beside two confused people on a road and opened the Scriptures to them until their hearts burned. Walk beside me. Open my eyes to what is actually there. When I reach the hard places, don't let me pretend they're easy, and don't let me quit.

Give me someone to read with, and enough light for the next step.

More than understanding, let me meet you. Let Jesus be the center of what I read, as he said he was. Make me someone this book can read, and not only someone who reads it. Amen.

faq.q: What book of the Bible should I read first?
faq.a: Start with the Gospel of Mark. It's the shortest of the four accounts of Jesus' life, sixteen chapters, and it moves quickly, so you can read it in about two weeks at a chapter a day, or in a single evening. Beginning with a Gospel means meeting the center of the Bible first; Jesus himself read the Scriptures as a story that led to him (Luke 24:27). Then read Genesis, where the story begins, with a psalm alongside for prayer or a chapter of Proverbs for everyday wisdom. After that, the eleven-act [Story of the Bible](/study/bible/story) on this site walks every chapter once.

faq.q: Which Bible translation should I read?
faq.a: Read one you understand. Some translations stay close to the wording of the Hebrew and Greek, word for word; others put the meaning into natural English, thought for thought. The ESV leans word for word, the NLT thought for thought, and the NIV aims for a balance between the two. The Berean Standard Bible, which this site's [Study Bible](/study/bible) uses, is a modern translation in the public domain. If you love the King James Version, keep it, with a modern translation beside it where its four-hundred-year-old English has shifted. Comparing two translations is one of the simplest ways to see what a hard verse is doing.

faq.q: How long should I read the Bible each day?
faq.a: Long enough to read a whole chapter or story without hurrying; ten or fifteen minutes is plenty to begin. A short time you keep will shape you more than an hour you abandon. Reading the whole Bible in a year takes a little over three chapters a day, since a Protestant Bible has 1,189 chapters, which makes a good goal for a second time through. Scripture sets no quota. It commends meditating on God's word day and night (Psalm 1:2), which is about nearness more than volume.

faq.q: What do I do with the violent parts of the Bible?
faq.a: Take them seriously, read them in their setting, and keep reading. The Bible doesn't hide its violence, and an honest reader shouldn't either. Some of it is simply reported, a record of how far people fell; some is presented as God's judgment, and those passages are genuinely hard. Ask who wrote the passage, to whom, what kind of writing it is, and where it sits in a story that leads to Jesus, who told his followers to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44). Christians have read these texts in more than one careful way, and the site's guide [Why Is the Old Testament So Violent? An Honest Look](/resources/context/the-violence-of-the-old-testament) is a good next step.

faq.q: How do I understand the Bible when it's confusing?
faq.a: Expect some confusion; even the Bible admits that parts of it are hard to understand (2 Peter 3:16). When you're stuck, ask who wrote the passage, to whom, what kind of writing it is, and where it sits in the Bible's one story. Read the whole chapter, use good notes (the [Study Bible](/study/bible) here has notes on every chapter), and compare a second translation. Then write your question down and ask someone who has read longer than you. Understanding usually comes slowly and in company, the way it came to two disciples on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:32).

faq.q: Can I read the Bible if I don't believe it?
faq.a: Yes. Read it the way you'd read any serious ancient book: carefully, honestly, and without pretending. You don't have to pray first or agree with anything, and I'd rather you read it as an honest skeptic than as a pretend believer. Start with Mark, write your objections down, and look up a passage's setting before you settle on a verdict. The Bereans in Acts are commended for examining the Scriptures every day to see whether what they heard was true (Acts 17:11). The site's plan for skeptics, [Eight Weeks of Reading Like an Adult](/plans/skeptic), was written for exactly this.

slots.note: James came to faith from atheism. If he wants, he could add in his own words what the Bible was like for him as a skeptic: where he first started reading, what he expected to find, what he actually found, and what kept him reading. The section stands without it.

On 2 Timothy 3: James was raised without a father. He could add, in his own words, what it meant to come to Scripture with no one in his family to hand it to him, and what it is like now to read it with his five sons. The reading stands without it.
What James's own daily reading looks like (the time, the place, the translation, what he does with his questions), if he is willing to share it.
Which translation James reads and preaches from, and why, in his own words. The translation answer describes the options fairly and names no choice for him.

sources.claim: The chapter divisions used in modern Bibles are traditionally credited to Stephen Langton, who taught in Paris before becoming Archbishop of Canterbury (1207). The attribution is contested: Paul Saenger and Laura Bruck, The Anglo-Hebraic Origins of the Modern Chapter Division of the Latin Bible (2008), trace the chapters to late twelfth-century England. The page therefore says traditionally credited and calls the chapters only medieval.
Robert Estienne's Greek New Testament of 1551 was the first to contain the modern system of numbered verse divisions.
sources.cite: Trinitarian Bible Society, The 1551 Greek New Testament of Stephanus

reviewed.notes: Second-pass editorial review, done in full from the top. Truth: every passage and inline reference re-read in the BSB with its chapter. Fixed: the Scripture intro said the Bible never treats needing help as shameful, but Jesus calls the Emmaus pair slow to believe (Luke 24:25), so it now says so and says neither is sent away; the Luke reading no longer puts the walk late on Easter and now ends on the recognition at the table (24:30-32); the Acts reading no longer asserts the official felt no embarrassment; the 2 Timothy reading calls the letter Paul's farewell rather than his last, and no longer claims 3:14 names Lois and Eunice, only that 1:5 says his faith lived first in them. History, confirmed by search against reference sources (the pages themselves are egress-blocked here): the chapters are now traditionally credited to Stephen Langton and called medieval, because Saenger and Bruck (2008) contest the attribution; Estienne's 1551 numbering is limited to the New Testament; copies of Tyndale's New Testament, not the book in the abstract, were burned in London in October 1526, and he was executed for heresy in 1536; Jeremiah's seventy years are Babylon's (29:10); believers hearing Scripture with someone to help them understand was narrowed to hearing it read aloud. Translations are described in terms their publishers use (ESV essentially literal, NLT thought for thought, NIV a balance of the two; the draft's tries to balance became aims for a balance); the BSB's public-domain dedication (April 2023) confirmed. Fairness: sixty-six books and 1,189 chapters now say a Protestant Bible; any modern translation became any major modern translation; the skeptic's objection is stated as an anthology by many hands, not a jumble; Why this is so hard no longer says the ancient world is rarely where people quit, which contradicted the Leviticus paragraph; Exodus added so the first paragraph does not skip from Genesis to Leviticus. Links: all 17 kit links opened at their manifests or components and every label matches (plan title per plans-index.json; eleven acts and all 1,189 chapters in story.json; Mark's intro and 16 chapter notes; 12 books in the Bible Study tool; the Story of the Bible guide says a volunteer can lead it with no preparation). The hotline link now goes to /help#help-now; 988 and the National Domestic Violence Hotline are both in crisis-resources.json. 2 Timothy and 2 Peter are still described as the letters present themselves, in line with the Study Bible's authorship notes. No statistics, no quotations but Scripture, no invented stories; first person appears only as self-implication (I'm a preacher) and one line of conviction to the skeptic. Slots unchanged (James's reading as a former atheist, reading Scripture as a man raised without a father and with his five sons, his own daily practice, his translation).
